summary: Initial POC scoping between Redwood and BrightHealth to decide between hosted, dedicated, and private deployment for a clinical-document summarization and QA workload. Key decision factors: latency (p95), cost per 1k requests, data residency/SOC2, predictable throughput for daily peak windows, and timeline for a 4-8 week pilot. Action items agreed: share security docs, customer to provide sample data, schedule benchmarking and dedicated trial for throughput verification.
topics: Workload sizing (tokens per request, concurrency, daily QPS)
Benchmark plan and metrics (p95 latency, throughput, per-token cost)
Deployment decision criteria (hosted vs dedicated vs private)
Timeline and next steps for pilot/POC
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-27
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 38 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jordan Patel (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (BrightHealth Head of ML), David Moore (Platform Eng), Ruth Lopez (Security), Tom Bryant (CTO)

Summary (auto): quick notes on deployment tradeoffs, ask for benchmark samples, plan dedicated pilot run.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Maya from Redwood here, I'm the AE, with Jordan, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Aisha Khan: Hi, thanks. We're good. We wanted to cover POC scope — we're trying to decide whether hosted or dedicate or private makes sense for our clinical summarization flow.
[00:14] Jordan Patel: Great, yeah we'll walk through the tradeoffs and then get to specific success criteria and a benchmarking plan. Quick ask up front — do you have a preferred timeline for the POC?
[00:22] Tom Bryant: We want something quick-ish; ideally a 4-week pilot to validate latency and cost, then a 4-8 week expansion if fine. But security approvals may push things.
[00:31] Ruth Lopez: Right, from security we need SOC2, audit logs, KMS integration, and proof of network isolation for PHI.
[00:39] Maya Chen: Totally understood. We'll share our SOC2 and ISO artifacts and a network diagram. For KMS we have integrations with common cloud KMS and HSMs.
[00:45] David Moore: For sizing — high level, our flow is clinical note ingestion -> summarization -> index/store -> QA assistant. The summarization step gets most tokens, average request is 1.5k tokens, peak concurrency around 60 requests/sec during nightly batch windows, steady state 8 QPS daytime.
[01:03] Jordan Patel: Helpful. So 1.5k tokens per request — do you have percentiles for longer tails? 95th?
[01:09] Aisha Khan: 95th is about 3k tokens, maybe 5k in some edge cases.
[01:14] Jordan Patel: Ok that matters for memory/KV cache. For a hosted approach we can serve that with autoscaling, but tail spikes could increase cost. Dedicated gives predictable throughput and better latency SLOs for p95 because you own the pool. Private gives max control but longer setup time.
[01:30] Tom Bryant: Can you quantify the p95 latency differences roughly?
[01:33] Jordan Patel: Ballpark: hosted API p95 for that token range could be 250-450ms depending on model and batching. Dedicated we typically see 150-300ms p95 because of reserved capacity and tuned compilation. Private (on-prem) depends on infra; with right GPUs you'd be in the 130-300ms p95 range but that requires your ops to manage quantization and kernel tuning. These numbers are approximate, we will bench them.
[01:58] Ruth Lopez: From compliance, hosted is easier for speed of onboarding but we need to ensure data retention and opt-out for logs. How long does Redwood keep logs by default?
[02:07] Maya Chen: Default retention is 30 days for request traces; we have enterprise options for longer retention and can disable storing request payloads. We'll put that in the security pack.
[02:15] Aisha Khan: Success criteria for us are accuracy of summaries (ROUGE-ish metrics and manual review), p95 latency under 300ms for interactive flows, and cost under $0.01 per inference on average. If we can't meet both latency and cost, we need a clear tradeoff.
[02:34] Jordan Patel: Good concrete goals. For cost we can model per-token cost with quantized models and batching — Redwood Optimize suggestions often find 30-50% savings with batching and KV prefix caching.
[02:44] David Moore: We also have a hard constraint: any PHI must not leave our VPC in production. For the POC we can use de-identified data, but ultimately the private or VPC-hosted options are preferred.
[02:57] Maya Chen: Understood. That's a common pattern — do a proof-of-value with de-id data on hosted or dedicated trial, then move to Private (VPC or on-prem) for production. We'll try to scope the POC to show both performance and a migration path.
[03:09] Tom Bryant: What about SLA expectations for dedicated?
[03:12] Maya Chen: Dedicated has SLA-backed uptime and latency targets in our enterprise contracts; we'll share typical numbers. For the pilot we can provide a limited-time dedicated pool for benchmarking.
[03:21] Jordan Patel: On benchmarks, here's what I propose: two runs — one synthetic run matching your token distribution (1.5k median, 95th 3k-5k) at different concurrencies (8, 60, 200) and one end-to-end with your de-id dataset through your ingestion pipeline hosted in your test account or our staging. We'll measure p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, and cost per inference.
[03:43] Aisha Khan: 200 concurrency sounds high — are you thinking burst testing? We do have nightly windows where internal throughput is high, but production interactive is lower.
[03:51] Jordan Patel: Yes that's burst/peak to validate autoscaling. Also we'll run a steady-state 8 QPS test for SLA-like expectations.
[03:58] David Moore: For VPC/private we need to know networking setup — does Redwood Private require specific firewall rules, egress?
[04:05] Maya Chen: For Private we provide a control plane and a data plane option. The data plane can run in your VPC and we support either private link or peering; we'll include the network diagram. Egress is controllable; you can restrict outbound, and logs can be sent to customer S3/Cloudwatch if needed.
[04:22] Ruth Lopez: And KMS integration? We need customer-managed keys.
[04:25] Maya Chen: Yes, we support KMS/HSM integration; we'll include docs and examples.
[04:30] Tom Bryant: Ok timeline — can we do a three-phase POC? Phase 1: hosted quick benchmark with de-id data (2 weeks). Phase 2: dedicated trial to validate p95 and cost (2-3 weeks). Phase 3: private/prod planning (4+ weeks) pending security sign-off.
[04:48] Maya Chen: That sequence makes sense. For Phase 1 we can spin up hosted test harness in days. For Phase 2 we need to allocate dedicated pool — that needs internal provisioning but we can target a week to spin up once we agree config.
[04:59] Jordan Patel: For the dedicated config we'll need to know model size preferences — do you have a target model or are you open to Redwood-curated variants?
[05:06] Aisha Khan: Prefer open models that are strong on summarization; the team likes Llama-3 style models or similar. We want to ensure medical text fidelity.
[05:14] Jordan Patel: We can recommend a few candidate models and a quantization profile. For clinical fidelity we often run a small human eval set during the POC. We'll coordinate prompt sets.
[05:25] Ruth Lopez: One question — audit logs for queries with PHI, do you redact them automatically?
[05:30] Maya Chen: We can disable request payload logging, and any logs kept can be redacted. We'll show controls in the security pack.
[05:36] Tom Bryant: Pricing — rough numbers for dedicated? per-hour GPU plus support?
[05:40] Maya Chen: Typically dedicated is a capacity commit (monthly) that maps to X GPUs for a pool; we provide a cost model in the pricing sheet. For the POC we can offer a limited trial discount. We'll send concrete numbers after this call.
[05:52] Aisha Khan: On benchmarks, we also want SLOs around tokenization and cold-start behavior — KV cache warm-up impacts p95 for longer sessions. Can you measure cold vs warm?
[06:04] Jordan Patel: Absolutely; we'll include cold-start and steady-state with cache-warm measurements. Also measure tail latencies.
[06:12] David Moore: For the test harness, can Redwood run the bench from our AWS account into a dedicated pool in Redwood Dedicated? We prefer the traffic originate from our VPC to avoid data egress policies.
[06:23] Jordan Patel: We can set that up with private connectivity. For hosted tests we'll do from Redwood staging. For dedicated we can either run our generators or give you the harness to run locally and post results.
[06:33] Maya Chen: Quick note — we'll need a primary contact from your side for infra requests. David, would that be you?
[06:38] David Moore: Yep I'll be primary infra contact.
[06:40] Maya Chen: Great. Questions from customer?
[06:43] Aisha Khan: Just one on evaluation: besides latency and cost we care about hallucination or factuality. How do you surface regressions?
[06:51] Jordan Patel: We have Redwood Optimize and eval tooling — you can upload prompts and references and run automated evals. We alert on regressions vs baseline and provide diffs. For POC we'll run a small manual eval plus automated metrics.
[07:04] Ruth Lopez: Anything in the call that would cause legal hold or contract negotiations early?
[07:08] Maya Chen: Not at this stage; we'll provide standard terms and a pilot agreement. If production goes private/dedicated we'll negotiate enterprise terms.
[07:16] Tom Bryant: Ok. Can you put together a simple success matrix — pass/fail criteria for moving from hosted pilot to dedicated full eval and then to private prod?
[07:24] Maya Chen: Yes we'll draft a success matrix: accuracy thresholds, p95 latency thresholds, cost per inference, security gates (SOC2, KMS), and operational readiness (monitoring/alerts).
[07:35] Aisha Khan: For cost target we said $0.01 per inference on average — is that realistic with 1.5k tokens?
[07:42] Jordan Patel: It may be tight at that token size on hosted without quantization; with aggressive quantization and batching we can often get closer. Dedicated tends to give better unit economics at scale. We'll model both.
[07:52] David Moore: Any gotchas with token accounting? We need clarity on how tokens map to our billing.
[07:57] Maya Chen: We'll include a pricing worked example that shows prompt/response tokens and prefix caching effects.
[08:02] Jordan Patel: A couple implementation notes — for recap: we'll run synthetic and real-data benches, capture p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, cost per inference, cold vs warm, and include caching effects. We'll also show Suggested batching and quantization profiles with expected cost delta.
[08:18] Aisha Khan: Sounds good. For data sharing — we'll provide deid samples OT via secure S3 link?
[08:23] David Moore: Yes, we'll put samples in an internal S3 bucket and share a pre-signed link.
[08:27] Maya Chen: Perfect. We'll need an IAM role or ephemeral creds for the harness if running from your account. We'll include instructions.
[08:34] Ruth Lopez: On the legal side, we need to know data processing addendum and any subprocessors.
[08:39] Maya Chen: We'll include DPA and subprocessors list in the security pack.
[08:44] Tom Bryant: Ok I think we have the outline. Anything else?
[08:47] Jordan Patel: One more technical thought — if you have very long context (>4k tokens) we might recommend segmented summarization and KV cache; we'll test both approaches.
[08:56] Aisha Khan: Yes some notes hit 10k tokens. We'll include representative cases.
[08:59] Maya Chen: Great. We'll produce an email with the plan and attach the security docs and benchmark runbook.
[09:04] Tom Bryant: Excellent. Thanks everyone.
[09:07] Maya Chen: Thanks all, we'll follow up with dates.

Notes on transcript quality: some product names were garbled in auto-transcription (e.g., "Redwood dedicate" for "Redwood Dedicated"). Natural speech disfluencies retained.

- Customer (Aisha/David) to share de-identified sample prompts and dataset + provide infra contact and network constraints by 2026-10-04.
- Schedule benchmark runs during week of 2026-10-11; Redwood to prepare bench harness and config by 2026-10-06.
